WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Pending cases in High Courts and Subordinate Courts 
*101. SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA: Will the Minister of 
LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of pending cases in various High Courts and 
Subordinate Courts in the country and the number of judges available to deal 
with them till 31 st December, 2001; 
(b) the norms* fixed for the number of judges as per 5/10 lakh 
population; and 
(c) the number of vacancies of judges lying vacant till date, State-wise, 
and by when it will be filled up, so as to dispose of pending cases in above 
mentioned court? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. JANA 
KRISHNAMURTHI): (a) to (c) The number of cases pending in the High Courts 
and Subordinate Courts are given at Statement I and II respectively (See below). 
The position regarding availability and vacancies of Judges in the High Courts 
and Subordinate Courts is indicated at Statement III. and IV respectively. (See 
below). 
The judge strength in High Courts and Subordinate Courts is not based 
on population. The review of judge strength of High Courts is undertaken 
every three years with reference tcUhe felt need for disposal of cases, taking 
into account the backlog and expected future filing. 
For filling up the existinig vacancies of 134 Judges/Additional Judges in the 
High Courts, 71 proposals as on July 17, 2002, are at various stages of 
consideration. The filling up of vacancies in the High Courts is a consultative 
process among the Constitutional authorities. While every efforts is made to fill 
up the existing vacancies expeditously, vacancies 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2002] 
do keep on arising on account of retirement, resignation or elevation of Judges. 
Therefore, it is not feasible to indicate the exact time by which the vacant 
posts are likely to be filled up. 
The Hon'ble Supreme Court, vide its judgement of 21 st March, 2002 in All 
India Judges' Association & Ors. Vs Union of India & Ors., has directed that 
the increase in the judge strength of Subordinate Courts to 50 judges per 10 lakh 
people should be effected and implemented with the filling up of the posts in a 
phased manner within a period of five years from the date of judgement. 
As regards District/Subordinate Courts, the Supreme Court, in All India 
Judges' Association & Ors. Vs. Union of India & Ors., has directed that the 
existinig vacancies in the Subordinate Courts at all levels should be filled if 
possible latest by 31 st March, 2003, in all the State. Minister of Law, Justice & 
Company Affairs vide his letter dated 26th April, 2002 has written to all the 
State Governments for taking early steps for filling up vacancies in the 
Subordinate Courts on priority. As regards Union Territories, necessary action has 
been initiated by the Central Government.

Expensive cancer treatment 
*102.   SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
SHRIBHAGATRAM MANHAR: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that treatment of cancer in the country is very 
expensive and is beyod the reach of poor and middle class people' 
(b) if so, whether Government have any plan to ensure that poor 
patients suffering from cancer are given treatment at nominal cost at 
12 

[22 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
various hospitals and institutes in Delhi; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) to (c) Keeping in view the expensive nature of drugs 
and equipments for cancer treatment, it is the endeavour of the Central 
Government and State Governments hospitals/institutions to provide cancer 
treatment either free or at nominal costs to be poor patients. With this objective, 
Central Government initiated National Cancer Control Programme 
(NCCP) in 1975.The emphasis is to ensure easy accessibility of cancer 
treatment facilities all over the country. Details of the National Cancer Control 
Programme are enclosed as Statement (See below). 
2. Besides Government run hospitals and medical college hospitals, 
19 Regional Cancer Centres have been set up under the scheme where 
treatment to poor patients is available either free or at nominal costs. 
Poor patients living below poverty line can also avail of financial assistance 
from National Illness Assistance Fund (NIAF) being operated by the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. 
3. In Delhi, the Institute Rotary Cancer Hospital in A.I.I.M.S. has 
been provided assistance of Rs. 42.60 crores and Safdarjung Hospital 
Rs. 3.25 crores for augmenting facilities for treatment of cancer in the 9th 
Five Year Plan. 
Statement 
National Cancer Control Programme 
Development of Oncology Wing in Medical College Hospital 
This scheme is available only for Government Medical Colleges to fill up 
the geographical gaps in the detection and treatment of cancer in the country. 
Financial assistance up to Rs. 2.00 crores  is provided to an institute under the 
scheme for purchase of equipments like Cobalt Machine, Brachytherapy etc. This 
is a one-time grant. 
Setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit 
Financial assistance up to Rs. 1.50 crore is provided to State 
Government for setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit in Government 
institutions. 
13 
34 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2002] 
An amount of Rs. 1.00 crore is provided for Cobalt Therapy Unit to the 
Non-Government Organisations. 
The Mammography equipments has also been included under the scheme 
for setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit. A Central assistance up to Rs. 30.00 lakhs 
is provided to those institutions/organisations who have the facilities for 
treatment of cancer patients and has well-equipped Radiotherapy Department. 
All these are on-time grant. 
District Cancer Control Programme 
A scheme of district project (duration-five years) for health education, 
detection and pain relief measures under National Cancer Control Programme 
was initiated during the year 1990-91. In this scheme, financial assistance of Rs. 
15.00 lakhs is provided to the State Qovemment/UT administration for each 
district selected under the scheme with a provision of Rs. 10.00 lakhs per annum 
for each district for the remaining four years of the project period. After five 
years, the project is to be taken over by the State ©overnment. 
Financial Assistance to Registered Voluntary Organisations 
Under the scheme assistance upto Rs. 5.00 lakhs is provided to the 
Voluntary Organisations tor undertaking health education and early detection 
activities in cancer on the specific recommendations of the State 
©overnments. 
Regional Cancer Centres 
This Ministry has recognised 19 Regional Cancer Centres in different 
States/UTs. The Chittaranjan National Cancer Institute, Kolkata and Institute 
Rotary Cancer Hospital (IRCH), AIIMS, New Delhi have got a different 
funding pattern. Remaining RCCs are paid an amount of Rs. 75.00 lakhs 
annually. These RCCs extend treatment facilities and conduct research in the 
field of cancer. 
UN Special Session on Children 
*103. SHRILAJPAT RAI: WiH the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
14 

[22 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that India had committed itself to meet the goals 
set at the 1990 World Summit for Children; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that a decade later, when the UN Special Session 
on Children met to review the progress on these commitments, India was 
among the defaulting nations; and 
(c) if so, the factors that led to not meeting he targets set particularly for 
nutrition and child health care? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRISHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) to (c) The first World Summit for Children 
held in 1990, adopted a Declaration that included goals for the survival, growth 
and development of children. The UN General Assembly Special Session on 
Children was held in New York from 8—10, May 2002, to review the 
achievements made by the member countries vis-a-vis \o the goals and to decide 
future plan of action. As per the "Progress-A Statstical Review" released by 
UNICEF for the UN General Assembly Special Session for Children, India's 
rate of progress regarding most indicators has been higher than the global 
average. 
Child health and nutrition indicators have improved. Substantial 
progress has been achieved in reducing the infant mortality rate. The infant 
morality rate declined from 114 per thousand live births in 1980 to 80 per 
thousand live births in 1990. Infant mortality rate further declined to 68 per 
thousand live births in the year 2000. Improvement has also been recorded in 
the nutritional status of children. The National Family Health Survey-2 (1998-
99) reported that the percentage of children who are underweight under are three 
years was 47 per cent as compared to 53 per cent reported by the National Family 
Health Survey-1 (1992-93).

Urban Development Reforms 
*108.   DR. T.SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: 
Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to during radical reforms to make civic 
bodies self-sufficient and self-reliant; 
(b) if so, whether a meeting of Housing and Urban Development 
Ministers of all States was held in the month of June, 2002 to discuss the urban 
Development reforms; 
(c) if so, the main decisions taken in the meeting; and 
(d) the steps being taken to implement them? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI ANANTH KUMAR): (a ) In order to make the civic 
bodies self-sufficient and effective, the Minister of Urban Development & 
Proverty Alleviation has taken the following initiatives for reforms in the 
urban sector:— 
(i) URBAN REFORMS INCENTIVE FUND 
In order to deal with the ever growing urban problems, in the Budget 
18 

[22 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
for the year 2002-2003, an Urnban Reforms Incentive Fund (URIF) with an initial 
outlay of Rs. 500 crore has been set up to provide reform linked assistance to 
the States. Planning Commission is evolving the modalities for the operation of 
the Fund. 
Urban Reforms Incentive Fund (URIF) will seek to intensify reforms in 
the following areas: 
* Reform of Rent Control Laws and repeal of Urban Land Ceiling Acts. 
* Rationalisation of high stamp duty regimes. 
* Revision of bye-laws to streamline the approval process for 
construction of buildings, development of sites, etc. 
* Revision of municipal laws in line with model legislation prepared by 
the Ministry of Urban Development & Poverty Alleviation. 
* Simplification of legal and procedural frameworks for conversion of 
agricultural land for non-agriculture purpose. 
* Levy of realistic user charges and resource mobilization by urban local 
bodies. 
* Initiation of Public Private partnership in the provision of civic 
services. 
(ii) CITY CHALLENGE FUND (CCF) 
It has also been announced in the Budget 2002-2003 that a City 
Challenge Fund will be set up as an incentive based grant facility that will 
support cities to fund transitional costs of moving towards sustainable and 
creditworthy institutional system of municipal management and service delivery. 
This Fund will meet the expenses to be incurred by the cities to finance the cost 
of developing a reform programme and its implementation. 
(iii) STATE-LEVEL POOLED FINANCING STRUCTURE 
It has also been announced in the Budget for 2002-2003 for setting of a 
Pooled Finance Development Fund to provide credit enhancement to assist local 
bodies to access market borrowings on a creditworthy basis through a State 
level intermediary. 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2002] 
(iv) TAX-FREE MUNICIPAL BONDS 
As an incentive for development of municipal bond market in India the 
Central Government gave fiscal concessions to the investors for investing in 
municipal bonds. 
In the fiscal year 2001 -2002 the Central Government allowed issue of tax-
free municipal bounds upto Rs. 200 crores. 
In the fiscal year 2002-2003, provisions has been kept for issue of Tax-
Free Municipal Bonds upto Rs. 500 crores. All State Government have been 
requested to sent the proposal for tax-free Municipal Bonds. 
(v) PROPERTY TAX REFORMS 
Though Property Tax (PT) is the most important tax source of revenue 
particularly for the municipal bodies of non-octroi States, Guidelines have been 
issued by the Ministry in 1998 for property tax reforms to all State 
Government with the objective of simplification and rationalizations of 
property tax. These measures are in the process of implementation by a number 
of States like Bihar. Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and 
Karnataka.

*114. SHRI RISHANG KEISHING: Will the Minister of

wise;

THE MINISTER OF DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH EASTERN 
REGION (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) The Department of Development of 
North-Eastern Region (DONER) was created in September, 2001 .The first 
budgetary allocation for the Department was made for Rs. 478.51 crores for 
the fiscal year 2002-03. A provision of Rs. 500 crores was made in the 
Demand for Grants relating to the Ministry of Finance in 2001 -2002 towards 
the Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources which is administered by DONER. 
(b) Some of the major thrust areas for economic development of North 
East consist of improving the infrastructure; providing greater access to basic social 
services like education, health, drinking water and sanitation etc.; expanding 
economic and social opportunities for all; building capacities aimed at increased 
efficiency; creating an environment for private 
23

participation conducive to growth; and providing a policy environment to 
positively influence wide ranging economic activities having employment/ 
income generation potential. 
(c) Funds are not allocated State-wise. Instead, project specific 
assistance is released for sanctioned projects under the Central Pool. The 
release of funds to the State Government depends on their capacity to formulate 
sound project proposals, utilize the funds released and the pace of 
implementation of the projects on the ground. 
(d) The projects are monitored by various agencies in the Union 
Government including through physical verification. Additionally, for each 
project, Quarterly Progress Report is obtained. Only after receipt of Utilisation 
Certificates, the second and subsequent instalments of project funds are released. 
Officers of this department have commenced field inspections of projects under 
execution. At the request of the department the Comptroller and Auditor 
General of India has agreed to undertake audit of some projects during their 
execution itself. The State Governments have also been advised to ensure that 
developmental projects are regularly monitored. 
Renewal of permission to Medical and Dental Colleges 
*115. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry has recently denied renewal of permission to 
several Medical and Dental Colleges in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the eligibility criteria in the recognised Medical and Dental 
Colleges have also been further revised; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the steps taken by Government to curb mushrooming of substandard 
Medical and Dental Colleges in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) and (b) As per provisions of Indian Medical 
Council (Amendment) Act, 1993 and the Dentists (Amendment) 
24 

[22 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Act, 1993 and the Regulations framed thereunder, the Central Government 
permission is granted for starting of a Medical/Dental College for one year. 
This permission is renewed on yearly basis after verification of the 
achievements of annual targets in respect of creation of infrastructure 
facilities. In case of failure of the college authorities to meet the annual target 
of development of infrastructure, the annual renewal of permission is not 
granted. The college accordingly cannot admit students unless they rectify the 
deficiencies to the satisfaction of the Professional Councils and the Government 
of India. 
Further, this process of renewal of permission is a continuous one and the 
Government renew the permission as and when the recommendations of the 
Professional Councils are received. As on date, permission to 27 medical and 
36 dental colleges has not so far been renewed for the year 2002-03. State-
wise names of medical and dental colleges wherein permission for 2002-03 has 
not been renewed are given in the Statement {See below). 
All the State Governments/Universities have been informed about the 
status of each college for admission during 2002-03. The State Government 
have also been advised to check from Government of India before allotting 
students to a medical/dental college within their jurisdiction whether permission 
has been renewed in respect of that particular College. The status of admission in 
medical and dental colleges has also been made available on this Ministry's 
website http://mohfw.nic.intor information of the general public which is 
continuously updated. The concerned professional councils have also been 
advised to caution public in respect of the colleges, which are eligible for 
admission during 2002-03. 
(c) and (d)The establishment of Medical College Regulation, 1999 and 
Dental College, Regulations, 1993 provides for eligibility criteria. No further 
change/revision has been made in the eligibility criteria. 
(e) With a view to stop mushroom growth of sub-standard medical/ dental 
colleges, the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 and the Dentists Act, 1948 
were amended in 1993 to provide for prior permission of the Central 
Government for establishment of medical and dental colleges.

Population explosion 
†*120. DR. ABRAR AHMED: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India is on the brink of population explosion; 
(b) whether it is a fact that if this trend continues then India would be the 
most populated country in the world by the year 2050; 
(c) whether after failing in all their efforts to control the situation 
Government have now finally sought the cooperation of private sector for this 
purpose; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) to (d) India's population on March 1, 2001 was 
102,7 crore.The census 2001 has revealed that the decline in average annual growth 
rate of population has been sharper during 1991—2001, as given in the Table 
below:  
Decade Growth Rate 
1961—1971 2.20% 
1971— 1981 2.22% 
1981— 1991 2.14% 
1991—2001 1.93% 
The current high population growth rate in some parts of the country is due 
to: 
• The large size of the population in the reproductive age group 
(estimated contribution 60%) 
• Higher fertility due to unmet need for contraception (estimated 
contribution 20%) 
• High wanted fertility due to prevailing high Infant Mortality Rate 
(IMR) and son preference etc. (estimated contribution about 20%) 
While in absolute terms, the population of India has increased by 180.6 
Millions during the decade 1991 —2001 however, the change in net addition has 
shown a steady declining trend starting from 1991. Undoubtedly, a 
combination of the population momentum and the method mix widely adopted 
for fertility regulation has ensured that the net 
†Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
36 

[22 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
additionally is on the decrease. For the country as a whole the achievements 
under the "National Family Welfare Programmes" have been quite substantial. 
Some States/UTs like Goa, Nagaland, Delhi, Kerala, Pondicherry, 
Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Tamil Nadu, Chandigarh and Mizoram have 
already achieved goals set for the year 2010 and States/UTs like Manipur, Daman 
& Diu, Kamataka, Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, West Bengal, 
Maharashtra, Punjab, Arunachal Pradesh and Lakshadweep are close to achieving 
the goals. However, other States are lagging behind primarily on account of slow 
achievements of socio-economic indicators. 
National Population Policy adopted in February, 2000, envisages 
partnership of non-Government voluntary organizations, the private corporate 
sector, Government, and the community towards the national effort for 
achieving early population stabilisation. The national programme to reach out to 
households cannot be sustained by Government alone. Triggered by rising 
incomes and institutional finance, private health care has grown significantly, 
with an impressive pool of expertise and management skills, and currently 
accounts for nearly 75 per cent of health care expenditures. The Government has 
involved Non-Governmental Organization (NGOs) for provisioning of service 
delivery in unserved and underserved population of the country. By now 
Government has recognized Mother NGO for 439 districts of the country, 
through which a network of 1,000 NGOs is now in place. Four Regional 
Resource Centres in Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Dindigul, have been 
recognized, which will help in capacity building of these NGOs. The 
Government also had detailed consultations with Rotary International, 
Confederation of Indian Industries (Cll), Federation of Indian Chambers of 
Commerce and Industry (FICCI) for their support in extending family welfare 
services in partnership with the Government.

Delhi High Court's direction on treatment facilities 
466. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Delhi High Court has recently directed Government tc 
address properly the issue of treatment facilities of the Central Government Employees 
(including pensioners) in private hospitals where the cases were referred by the C.G.H.S. 
authorities; 
71 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2002] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether follow-up action has been taken in this regard to give effect 
to the High Court directive; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) The Hon'ble Delhi High 
Court vide judgement dated 30.5.2002 in Civil Writ Petition No. 4754/1996 filed 
byT.S. Oberoi versus Union of India and another had given observations and 
directions in para 11 of the said order as under:— 
"In may view, it is high time that the Central Government/CGHS 
authorities, while conferring the status of recognised Government speciality hospital 
should renegotiate the package rates for various procedures and treatments. The 
private hospitals receive several benefits from the State in terms of allotment of 
land at concessional rates, exemption or benefits of concessional custom duties 
in import of surgical, diagnostic, medical and other equipments and 
consumables. More often than not the stipulations and directive to the private 
hospitals for providing a certain percentage of free rooms or treatment for 
economically weaker sections are not implemented. A large number of 
Government and public sector employees are referred to private speciality 
hospital for treatment. It is for the CGHS authorities to negotiate with the private 
hospitals from a position of strength, so that discounter package rates and 
advantegeous terms are offered to employees for different procedures 
irrespective of some individual variation in the treatment. The authorities can 
also endeavour to have a modified package for cases entailing extra stay or 
repeat procedures. This is especially so, when the public hospitals are not in a 
position to cater to the requirements and meet the ever increasing demand with 
adequate facilities not being available. An earnest endeavour is required on the part of 
the Central Government to arrive a better negotiated terms for itself and its 
employees." 
In view of the above, the Hon'ble Court vide para 13 of the order has 
directed the respondents viz. Union of India to file an action taken report in 
respect of the observations and directions given in para 11 of the order brought 
out above, within four months from the date of order (30.5.2002). 
72 

[22 July, 2002]                  RAJYA SABHA 
(c) and (d) The Government while recognising private hospitals under 
CGHS Delhi, have signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) with the 
hospitals. One of the conditions in the MoA is that the private hospitals/ 
diagnostic centres recognised under CGHS will not charge more than the 
ceiling rates fixed by the CGHS for various medical procedures/tests/ 
investigations in O.M. dated 7.9.2001 for a period of two years from the date 
of issue of the O.M. Further, all future recognition of private hospitals under 
CGHS, Delhi would be in accordance with the provisions contained in the 
MoA. 
Hon'ble Delhi High Court has given four months time to the U.O.I, to 
file an ATR on the orders given on 30.5.2002.

479. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Delhi Police have unearthed fake drugs worth Rs. 60 crores 
from a spurious drug manufacturing unit which was being run in the capital; 
(b) if so, whether these consignments are being sold in the shops in rural 
areas and slums of the city; 
(c) whether a number of factories have been found using spurious drugs 
in the State; and' 
(d) if so, the steps being taken by Government to check the fake drug 
rackets operating in the market? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Delhi Police in association with 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2002] 
Drugs Control Department of Government of NCT (Delhi) had jointly 
unearthed an inter-state spurious drug racket clandestinely manufacturing, selling 
and distributing fake medicines. The police seized large stocks of the allegedly 
spurious drugs from different godowns in and around Delhi on July 4,2001. As 
per the information available, they recovered stocks/ seized drugs worth Rs. 
3.16 crores (approximately) and machinery of approximate value of Rs. 75.00 
lakh. In another raid on February 16, 2002, Delhi Police associated with the 
Officers of Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), seized a haul 
of fake drugs worth Rs. 36 lakhs (approximately) moving in inter-State 
commerce. Delhi Police have also unearthed a case on May 20,2002. They have 
reported that a large consignment of spurious drugs was seized from the 
godowns of M/s. Sri Krishna Air Services, Teliwara. 
(b) Under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules 
thereunder, the responsibility for regulating the manufacture and sale of Drugs 
as well as monitoring their quality is vested with the State Government. The 
State Drug Controllers have been asked to alert their inspectorate staff about 
possible inter-State movement of spurious drugs unearthed and detected in the 
raids carried out so that the same are not available with the chemist shops in 
the areas urjder their jurisdiction.

investigation revealed that 3 factories located at Shalimar Gaon, Delhi, Panipat, 
Haryana and Sharanpur, U.P., were reportedly clandestinely 
manufacturing/Trading drugs of questionable quality. 
(d) Since manufacture and sale of spurious drugs is mainly a 
clandestine activity, State Drug Control Organisations who are responsible 
to enforce the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetic Act, 1940 and Rule 
made thereunder have been advised to adopt following guidelines:— 
1. (a) It has been recommended to set up/reactivate State Drugs 
Advisory Committee in which all stakeholders, are partners, (b) 
Establishment of separate intelligence-cum-legal machinery with 
Police assistance (c) Speedy analysis of drug samples (d) To 
undertake surveillance of suspected dealers (e) To obtain cooperation 
of pharmaceutical industries (f) To collect survey samples under 
National Survey Quality Evaluation of Drugs (NSQED) Programme.

Steps to check population growth 
480.    SHRIMATI ABMIKA SONI: 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have pointed out that States have not taken serious 
steps to check the population growth; 
(b) if so, whether a number of States have prepared policies that propose 
various disincentives,, including denial of free rations and education to the third 
child; 
(c) if so, the States which have, so far, formulated the policy and those 
which have nor, and 
(d) the action being considered by Government against those States which 
have not taken measures to check the population growth? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) The Central Government reviews 
87 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2002] 
from time to time with the State Governments the progress made in various 
family welfare programmes. The States of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Goa, 
Nagaland, Delhi, Pondicherry, A&N Islands, Chandigarh and Mizoram have 
made considerable progress and have already achieved the replacement level 
of fertility, and have to sustain the progress. Current demographic trends 
indicate that 12 States and Union Territories of Karnataka, Andhra Pradsh, West 
Bengal, Maharashtra, Punjab Himachal Pradesh, Orissa, Manipur, Arunachal 
Pradesh, Lakshadweep, Daman and Diu and Sikkim are^Jkely to achieve 
replacement level early. However, Uttar Pradesh,'"Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, 
Rajasthan, Assam, Haryana, Gujarat, Tripura, Meghalaya, Jammu and 
Kashmir, Dadra and Nagar Haveli have to make special effort with improved 
primary health care services for accelerating implementation of programmes 
of population stabilisation. The Union Government and State Governments are 
making concerted efforts for improved coverage and outreach with an 
expanded package of services to achieve immediate objective of replacement 
level of fertility i.e. TFR of 2.1 by 2010 as mentioned in National Population 
Policy adopted by the Government in February, 2000. 
(b) to (d) State Population Policies have been adopted by Andhra Pradesh 
(1997), Rajasthan (December 1999), Madhya Pradesh (January 2000), Uttar 
Pradesh (July 2000), and Gujarat (March 2002) with state specific goals and 
strategies. All the States have been advised to devise their strategies and 
programmes in harmony with the National Population Policy, 2000 for reducing 
birth rates and achieving population stabilization. The national policy does not 
envisage any disincentives, as they tend to be coercive. To enhance and 
accelerate performance in States with currently below average socio-
demographic indices, an Empowered Action Group (EAG) has been constituted 
in the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for preparation of area specific 
programmes. A detailed database for eight States i.e. MP, UP, Bihar, Rajasthan, 
Orissa, Chhattisgarh, Uttaranchal and Jharkhand has been compiled by the 
Department of Family Welfare to help guide the assessment of community 
needs. This will facilitate rational and optimal utilization of resources in terms 
of reproductive health care products, services as well as public/NGO/private 
partnerships.

Focal Points for plague bacteria 
486. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the medical experts have identified four areas 
in the country which are focal points for plague bacteria; 
(b) if so, the details of the areas; 
(c) the criteria for the identification of these areas as focal points; and 
(d) the preventive measures taken in these areas to prevent the outbreak of 
the deadly disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELAFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The focal points for 
plague exist at the tri-junction of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kamataka 
and also in the State of Maharashtra, Gujarat and Himachal Pradesh. 
(c) * Cases of plague were reported from the above areas during the 
pandemic from 1889-1950. 
* Case of human plague was reported from Mulbagal, Kolar district in 
Kamataka in 1966. 
* Serosurveillance for plague showed antibodies against Y pestis (PJague 
organism) in rodents in the tri-junction of Kamataka, Tamil Nadu and 
Andhra Pradesh. 
* Outbreak of plague in Gujarat and Mahrashtra in 1994. 
* Suspected outbreak of plague in 1983 and confirmed outbreak of plague in 
2002 Himachal Pradesh. 
104 

[22 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
* Field Unit of National Institute of Communicable Diseases (NICD) 
located at Bangalore coordinates surveillance of plague in endemic States 
like Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Gujarat, 
Surveillance comprises of serological, entomological and bacteriological 
study. After 1994, no human plague cases have been reported from 
any of these States 
* The representatives from various endemic States are called in the 
inter-State plague coordination meetings to review the status of plague 
surveillance. The last such meeting was held in April, 2002 at Plague 
Surveillance Unit, Bangalore. 
* The State of Himachal Pradesh has been advised to establish a State 
Plague Surveillance Unit for which all technical help would be 
extended by NICD, Delhi. 
* For making prompt reliable diagnosis of the disease, a state-of-the-art 
laboratory, meeting all safety and diagnostic criteria of WHO is in 
existence at NICD, Delhi.

High-tech drug for Diabetes 
489. SHRIYADLAPATIVENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that a new high-tech drug is proving 
effective for all types of diabetes and is reducing dependence on insulin shots 
in the USA; 
(b) if so, whether Government are taking steps to make this drug 
available in the country; and 
(c) the other details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) According to Indian Council of 
Medical Research (ICMR), Thiazolidinedidne derivatives with insulin 
sensitizing activity such as troglitazone, rosiglitazone and pioglitazone lower 
the blood levels of glucose, free fatty acides and triglycerides and appear to 
reduce insulin resistance, possibly by increasing the activity of insulin receptor 
kinase. These drugs have been approved for use in obese 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2002] 
patients with non insulin dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM or Type 2-
Diabetes) who are poorly controlled on insulin and they have also been used by 
some physicians as an add on agent in NIDDM patients who are on maximal 
doses of other oral agents. Rosiglitazone and pioglitazone are already available 
in the Indian Market. 
Ban of use of animals for medical purposes 
490. SHRIRAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that present ban on use of animals for research and 
medical purposes has badly affected production on BCG Vaccine, thereby 
jeopardizing National Immunization Programme and production of venom 
antidote and several other crucial vaccines; 
(b) if so, what action has Government taken to resolve the issue; and 
(c) by when these laboratories are likely to get their full requirement of 
animals, etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA) (a ) to (c) The communication dated 
30.1.2002 of Committee for the Purpose for Control and Supervision of 
Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA) directing BCG vaccine laboratory, 
Chennai (the sole manufacturer of BCG Vaccine in India) to suspend 
experiments on guinea pigs would have definitely resulted in jeopardisation of 
BCG Vaccine supply to the National Immunization Programme had the Hon'ble 
High Court of Judicature, Chennai not intervented in the matter and issued a 
Stay Order dated 8.4.2002 on CPCSEA's communication dated 30.1.2002. 
Similarly, the production and testing of vaccines and antisera has been 
badly affected at Central Research Institute, Kasauli such as: 
* The production of Anti Snake Venom Serum and Anti Rabies Serum 
has been stopped since December, 2001. 
* Japanese Encephalitis production enhancement is hampered due to non-
availability of mice from other sources. 
* The final release of vaccine/anti-sera for commercial use is being 
affected as the testing of vaccine/anti-sera depends on the use of small 
animals such a guinea pigs.

494. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether as per World Bank study, 40,000 people die of air-pollution every 
year in Ahmedabad : Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi, Kanpur and Nagpur, besides 
Delhi, heads the list of such deaths; 
(b) whether air-pollution has a significant impact on heart disease and 
results in raise of coronary events within 24 to 48 hours after the pollution 
level increases in Delhi; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) The World Bank Study estimate of 
premature deaths is based on a model developed for other countries and 
applied to India. Therefore, it is very difficult to accept that these deaths are 
due only to pollution and not to any other factors. 
(b) Air pollution, specially Suspended Particulate Matters (SPM) is 
known to have impacts on health, mainly on the respiratory system which can in 
turn affect the heart. Under normal conditions only prologned exposure 
results in aggravation of the disease. 
(c) The Government has already implemented certain control measures 
such as introduction of:— 
(i) Unleaded petrol 
(ii) Bharat I and II emission standards 
(iii) Low sulphur diesel 
(iv) CNG for commercial vehicles 
(v) Pollution Under Control (PUC) certificate 
Central Pollution Control Board, Delhi is the authority for checking the 
air pollution levels in various cities and for studying the effect of various 
control measures through the concerned State Pollution Control Boards.

(d) the concrete steps Government propose to take to meet the 
situation and also to reduce the arrears in various courts in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. JANA 
KRISHNAMURTHI): (a) The total number of cases pending with the various High 
Courts and District/Lower Courts are at Statement I and II as per available 
information (See below). 
150 

[22 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) The main reasons for delay in the judgement, inter-alia, include 
shortage of judges, delays in process service and adjournment of cases. 
(c) and (d) The Supreme Court has been expeditiously disposing of 
pending cases. The Government have been compiling annual reports on 
pendency of cases in High Courts and District Courts and forwarding them to 
the High Courts for their information and necessary action. The High Courts 
have been requested to implement the recommendations of the Malimath 
Committee to streamline procedure which will, inter-alia, expedite disposal 
of pending cases. Further, the Government have also been constantly 
reviewing the accumulation of arrears in courts. Besides increasing the Judge 
strength from time to time, the Government have set up/encouraged 
alternative modes of dispute resolution including concilliation, mediation, and 
arbitration. Special tribunals like Central Administrative Tribunal, State 
Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tribunals, Labour Courts, 
Consumer Courts, etc. have been set up to expedite disposal of cases. 
Information technology is being used in generation of causelists, providing 
information to the litigants/Advocates etc. for speedy disposal of cases. Pilot 
project for the District Courts has been started for computerisation of City 
Courts in the four major metro cities of Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai. 
Fast Track Courts have been set up for quick disposal of long pending 
cases, priority being accorded to sessions cases pending for two years or more 
and cases involving undertrials in jails. All Central Ministries/Departments 
have been requested to take necessary steps like review of Acts/Laws 
administered by them, filing of counter-affidavits in time and avoidance of 
unnecessary adjournments in cases where they are a party. 
Civil Procedure Code has been amended and the amendments have 
been brought into force with effect from 1.7.2002 which, inter-alia, limit the 
number of adjournments which can be granted to a party to three, provide for 
speedy process service by speed post, courier services, fax or e-mail, 
authorise the court to fix time limit for oral arguments and provide for a 
number of other measures aimed at ensuring expeditious disposal of cases.

555. SHRI C. P. THIR UNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of

DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. 
RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (d) Provision of amenities such as drinking water, 
sanitation, traffic arrangement and health services in small and medium towns 
and cities is a State subject and hence State Government/Union Territories are 
to assess the amenities available in small and medium towns. 
The planning, implementation, operation and maintenance and 
provision of funds is also the responsibility of the concerned State

Based on the Information furnished by different State implementing

In order to supplement the efforts of the State Governments in providing 
water supply facilities, a Centrally Sponsored Accelerated Urban Water Supply 
Programme (AUWSP) for small towns having population less than 20,000 as 
per 1991 census was launched by the Ministry of Urban Development and 
Poverty Alleviation in 1993-94. Under this programme Central assistance is 
provided to the State Governments for implementation of water supply schemes 
in small towns on 50:50 funding pattern between Centre and State. As on 
30.6.2002, the Ministry has approved water supply schemes for 672 towns with 
an estimated cost of Rs. 848.42 crores and had released a Central share of Rs. 
360.57 crores to different State Governments since the launching of the 
programme. A Statement indicating the State-wise status of schemes approved 
under AUWSP, their estimated cost, funds released by the Ministry as Central 
share, expenditure reported by the State Governments, etc., is placed at 
Statement-ll (See below). 
The scheme of low cost sanitation for liberation of scavengers to 
completely eliminate the practice of manual scavenging by conversion of dry 
latrines into low cost water-seal pour-flush latrines and construction of new 
sanitary toilets. The scheme is being operated through the HUDCO by providing 
subsidy from the Central Government and loan from HUDCO to the States and 
Union Territories. This scheme is applicable to towns having population less 
than 5 lakhs as per 1981 census. 
Upto 30th June 2002, 858 schemes in 1492 towns have been sanctioned 
under which 36, 71,723 dry latrines/pour flush toilets would be converted/ 
contructed and 1,17,892 manual scavengers will get liberated after 
completion of 858 schemes. An amount of Rs. 511.68 crores has been 
sanctioned as subsidy and Rs. 514.98 crores as loan from HUDCO for these 
schemes. Out of this. Rs. 254.72 orores as subsidy and Rs. 314.78 crores as 
loan have been released by HUDCO to different States. So far, 
conversion/construction of 4,58,274 units have been completed and 3,19,041 
are in progress. 387 towns have been declared scavenger-free. 
In addition, the Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns 
(IDSMT) Scheme is one of the Centrally Sponsored Schemes under which 
financial assistance is given to towns upto 5 lakhs population as per 1991 census 
to take up the infrastructure development in these towns.

priority to the needs of the Urban Poor and response to their needs by the State

590. SHRI K.M. KHAN: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT
